title: Minimax Regret for Gini Welfare with Disparity Penalties and a Rare Protected Group
banked_reason: Delivered tier subfield below novelty_target field (floor field); not salvageable within scope.
gap_reasons: The claimed computational contribution is narrower: it establishes convergence of exhaustive discretized programs conditional on a valid numerical solve, but reports no instantiated outward-rounded certificate or computed value of the full V_J(kappa).
proof_attempt_summary: Discovery established a same-class finite-table minimax regret rate, an empirical-table upper rule, an all-procedure switching lower bound, and a marked-Poisson critical-count comparison; the mathematics referee passed with no findings. The cold tier review capped the delivered package at subfield because it lacked an instantiated full-value computation, scalable J=4 computation, and application calibration. A decision-referee related-work comparison remains to be written, but that prose repair cannot clear the field floor; no Lean formalization was launched.
tldr: A protected group whose expected record count is \(np\) creates an information bottleneck for the exact Gini-welfare objective penalized by protected-group Kolmogorov--Smirnov disparity. Over the stated binary finite-table randomized experiment, the all-observed-procedure minimax regret is \(\Theta(\min\{1,(np)^{-1/2}\})\): a projected empirical-table maximizer attains the upper rate, and a legal Bernoulli switch yields the matching converse. When \(np\to\kappa\), the full finite-table-class minimax risk converges to \(V_J(\kappa)\), a revealed-common-table marked-Poisson decision value. A loss-specific two-sided comparison and a finite-grid/count-truncation theorem give a convergent enclosure scheme and jointly Borel near-minimax kernels; an instantiated outward-rounded value certificate, the exact least-favorable support, and scalable full \(J=4\) computation remain open.
gap: Kock and Preinerstorfer (2026, Theorem 3.1) prove an empirical-policy upper bound whose constant deteriorates with protected-group mass, but they neither show that this dependence constrains every procedure nor characterize the bounded-count decision problem. Gaussian local treatment-rule theory and exact finite binary games do not cover the marked-Poisson likelihood and nonlinear Gini--Kolmogorov--Smirnov loss.
fill: A uniform switch proves the protected-mass lower rate, an empirical finite-table rule attains it, independent common-record prefixes and binomial--Poisson coupling compare the original and limiting risks, and a risk-modulus-based finite linear program gives certified value bounds and measurable near-minimax transfer rules.
